title: Inside the Mind of a Cop Killer
article: Robert Sand's friends thought of him as a quiet, cool-headed criminal and lady's man. But this was just one of the masks adopted by the Westlock, Alta., man who hunted down and killed a veteran Mountie.

WINNIPEG - Robert Marlo Sand shuffles into a visiting booth, his hands in cuffs, his legs in chains. He has requested this meeting at Manitoba's Stony Mountain Penitentiary, rather than just being interviewed over the phone for hours.
"I'd prefer to be able to look in your eyes," he says.

Sand, 24 years old and serving a life sentence for the first- degree murder of RCMP officer Dennis Strongquill, sits down in a chair and looks through a thick plastic divider. For the next hour, he speaks mostly in a low monotone, his dark eyes often unfocused. At five-foot-nine, he's of average height, but his shoulders and arms are massive, built up from 2,000 push-ups a day. He wrapped these same muscular arms around the neck of his own lawyer during his trial, a violent outburst that terrified his own lover Laurie Bell and every other courtroom spectator.
As he talks, Sand often flexes those muscles. At times he appears to tremble, as if he's fighting to keep something in check. Asked about this, he acknowledges he's struggling right now.
"I don't think I should be in a cage," he says. "I think the hardest thing to control is my need to respond."
Sand describes this need to respond as a demon looking over his shoulder, compelling him to lash out whenever he feels threatened.

"If I don't watch myself, I respond. If someone is joking around and gives me a shove, or does something threatening, then sometimes I can just respond. It's just an instinct. It's there. I just act."
He yearns to escape, he says. "If there is the slightest chance that I could walk out these doors right now, I'd jump all over it."

The demon that plagues Robert Sand leaves many people baffled. His crimes seem inexplicable. Why shoot at a police cruiser when you get pulled over for a routine traffic violation? Why hunt down the police? Why ram their cruiser, then gun down one of the officers?

The police investigated Sand for months and the justice system conducted a three-month trial, but at Sand's sentencing hearing, Justice John Menzies admitted he was still perplexed about the killer's motivations. "You're not a stupid man," Menzies told Sand. "You're an intelligent man. You can rationalize. You can feel for others. The only conclusion I can come to is you hate society. You can't tolerate authority. . . . You hate the police. I don't know why."

If anyone has answers, it's Sand himself, who didn't testify at his own trial or speak at his sentencing hearing. He's talking now however, and as he tells his story, a certain deadly equation becomes clear: Sand hates the police, feels justified in his hatred, and justified using violence. But while he rationalizes his war with the police, Sand is troubled by inklings of conscience and by the baggage of his violent teenage years.

He understands he's done wrong. Most painful for him is the realization other people would have been better off if they'd never known him, including Laurie Bell, now in jail on a manslaughter conviction, and his brother Danny, shot dead by RCMP snipers shortly after the Strongquill slaying. All the wrong that he's done, and convinced others to do, has made him poisonous, Robert believes.
"All that stuff is the poison, the poison within that secretes out my pores and infects everybody else around me," he says.

It's tempting to label a killer such as Sand as amoral, but, as Menzies noted, Sand can discern right from wrong. In fact, he lives by a rigid moral code, though the code is both extreme and skewed. He tends to see the world in a black-and-white fashion and delivers harsh, arrogant judgments about teachers, religion, police, society. Yet he can be equally hard on himself.

Born on Dec. 21, 1978, Sand is the eldest of three sons of Dennis and Elaine Sand and grew up in Westlock, a town 60 kilometres north of Edmonton. The Sand boys were all domineering, Dusty, the youngest of the three, has said. "We were prideful and we didn't take crap from anybody. We were raised to push our limits."
By junior high, Robert was committing break and enters.

Dennis Sand, the father, had his own troubles with the law as a young man, serving time for break-and-enter robberies before coming to understand there was no advantage to the criminal life, just conflict and uncertainty. Dennis became a handyman, working on farms and later for the County of Westlock. He's blunt, but most neighbours speak well of him.

Robert recalls with obvious admiration how at family gatherings his dad stood up to other men who misbehaved, including one man who abused a girlfriend. Dennis punched one of these offenders through a plate-glass window, Robert says. "The message I got from that is you should stand up for people that are vulnerable."

Robert's hatred of the police is also rooted in his father's experiences. Because of his dad's criminal record, police would always pull Dennis over and harass him, according to Robert. "He'd get pissed off, but I could see he wasn't afraid of them," Robert says, again with obvious admiration.
Several shattering events appear to have unhinged Sand during his teenage years.

According to Sand, the first occurred when he was about 14 years old in 1994. That year, he claims, he killed a man in self-defence. The RCMP have investigated this claim, but have so far found nothing to corroborate Sand's story.

Sand says he was going out to the countryside to pick up some drugs from someone involved in the drug trade. As always, he carried a knife for protection. When they met, the drug dealer had a firearm, a shovel and a bag of lye, to help dispose of a body. "I have no doubt he came there prepared to turn me into into dust," says Sand. The man wanted to kill him, he says, to make a point with someone who knew Sand.
But Sand says he turned the tables on the man, killing him instead.

The killing pushed him away from others, Sand says. To hide his savage side from others, he started to wear masks, as he puts it. "That's when I decided I had a need for the masks. Everybody thought I was being destroyed by drugs when it was actually something else. And then when I was quiet and more secretive, they all said that I was being paranoid and depressed.

"I had to develop the masks to put aside everyone's concerns, to let the family see that I was still there, and to be able to communicate with citizens. And, of course, you need a mask to hide your hate when you're dealing with the police. It's not always smart to let that hate show through."

As a result of all that's happened, Sand believes he's different than other people. "It's just a sense of being in a crowd but alone, of not belonging, probably from wearing too many masks for so long.
"It's all pretty confusing, not so much when you're wearing a mask because you just get absorbed into that character, but once you take them off, who are you, you know?"

One trauma suffered by Sand is well-documented, his best friend Richard Ford's death from an asthma attack. At the time of his death, Richard was 16, a tall, handsome kid, an excellent athlete, popular with girls and liked by many adults.

On the night of Aug. 20, 1995, Richard, Robert and some other teens were out partying at the Westlock town fair, drinking beer and smoking drugs, when Richard had a severe asthma attack. The kids rushed to the local hospital, but it was closed for the night and they had to bang hard and long on the locked doors to get the staff's attention. Medical intervention came too late. Richard died before Robert's eyes. Family and friends say Robert was never the same after that, becoming more reckless and depressed and falling deeper into drugs and crime.

In his circle, Robert was known as a quiet, cool-headed criminal and a lady's man. One night, he cheated on his main girlfriend with a new girl in town, Laurie Bell, who had left home in nearby Athabasca at age 15 to live with the drug crowd in Westlock. He and Bell got together at a house party.

"We sat up drinking and talking all night," Robert says. "Everybody else passed out and we had sex in the living room in a reclining chair, and we had a water fight naked in the kitchen, and we stayed up until the sun come up and we broke the reclining chair."

The Westlock drug crowd had a bad attitude about the police, one member of the group, Darren Peacock, has said. "A police officer was more of a concept than a person . . . The cops are the enemy, the wall between him and a big bag of loot and wanting to spend it all."
Robert Sand's hatred for police was stoked by various run-ins, in which he alleges the police used violent tactics in making arrests.

In October 1998, two months short of his 20th birthday, Sand was sentenced to seven years for various crimes, including stealing and torching a number of vehicles, two armed robberies, and resisting arrest by taking the police on a long chase down gravel roads.
On Nov. 1, 2001, he was granted day parole from Drumheller Institution and was sent to a half-way house, the Stan Daniels Healing Centre in Edmonton.

In late November 2001, Sand was walking Edmonton's downtown streets when he met up with his old lover, Laurie Bell. Addicted to crystal meth and deeply into the rave party scene, Bell was skinny and sick. "She was so unhappy," Sand says. "She was unclean."

Sand usually has no use for junkies, finding them weak and contemptible. But despite her addiction, Sand thought Bell was beautiful and attractive, so he decided to help her get off drugs. But Robert ran into trouble as he tried to balance his new relationship with Bell, his work, and the rules at Stan Daniels. A misunderstanding led him to miss curfew. He was grounded until the situation could be reviewed, but before that happened, he fled the half-way house on Dec. 12, 2001.

On the run, he was joined by his brother Danny, 21, who was also recently out of jail, having been imprisoned for almost running down a police officer while trying to evade arrest for a stealing a truck.
Together, with Bell, the Sand brothers set off on their crime spree, stealing guns, ammunition and vehicles and robbing a bank in Thorhild, Alta.

On the evening of Dec. 20, the threesome drank hard liquor and drove around the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border, trying to hunt down some pot. They ended up at a bar in Russell, Man., then headed out again around midnight, as it began to snow heavily.

Robert says he was too drunk to drive, so Danny took the wheel of the stolen truck. The threesome were travelling down back roads, Robert says, coming up to a highway. "I remember Dan said, 'Cops!' And right away my head, I wouldn't say it cleared, but my war mask come up, right up, right away."

RCMP Constables Brian Auger and Dennis Strongquill had noticed the Sand truck didn't stop when it merged on to the highway, then kept its high beams on as it passed. The officers decided to pull over the vehicle for a routine check. It was 12:30 a.m.
"Dan started to get agitated. I said, 'Stay calm. Just pull over.' "

Sand made some quick calculations. He didn't want to get into a police chase, not with Dan driving. Plus Bell had been in car accidents before and was paranoid about crashing. He had experience with gunfights, so he calmly got out and fired four shotgun blasts at the RCMP cruiser, hitting the hood, windshield and passenger door.
"I just wasn't in the mood to be hunted. So I made the decision to stop the truck and get out, and stop their truck, end the chase before it started."
At once, the police cruiser turned and sped away toward the town of Russell.

It was Dan's decision to turn the truck around and pursue the police cruiser, Robert says. "Maybe he was tired of being chased. I know I sure as hell was . . . They think we had it all planned out, but there was no conversation really."
At high speed, Danny caught up to the RCMP cruiser, following bumper-to-bumper. Robert leaned out the window and fired, blasting the police vehicle through its back window.
On his police radio, Strongquill shouted, "Shot at, we're being shot at guys. You hear that shootin' us? They're still shootin' us."

The cruiser stormed into Russell's RCMP detachment, slammed down a ditch and across the lawn, then skidded sideways before coming to a stop. Danny followed it, smashing into the side of the vehicle. Robert took aim and fired four blasts.
On the highway his intent had been to disable the cruiser, he says, but the circumstances had changed.
"There was shots coming from (the police)," Sand claims. "It was a full-out battle."
And his intent? "To survive, to win. They're shooting at me, I'm shooting at them. Their intent is the same thing."
Strongquill's gun malfunctioned, so he couldn't fire back. He wildly twisted and thrashed about as he tried to escape, but was fatally wounded by blasts to his back and sides.

Sand wasn't ashamed of the shootout. He continues to hold tight to his hate, to all the alleged wrongs the police have done to him, his dad, his friends. "I'm sorry Strongquill died as a man, and I feel for his family, but he was still in that uniform. I have no sympathy for that uniform at all."
The Sands fled through the night, stealing more trucks, torching them, firing on a farmer who gave chase, and also firing toward another police officer.

At a motel in Wolseley, Sask., they slept through the morning and early afternoon. By then, their truck had been identified. An RCMP tactical unit had almost encircled the motel when Robert looked out the front window and spotted a police vehicle and heavily armed snipers on the highway. Sand told Danny that police were outside and would soon be coming in. "I was suggesting that we shoot our way out of there. That's what he was prepared to do from the very beginning."

Sand kicked out the back window of the motel, then climbed out, shotgun in hand. Bell and his brother followed, Danny carrying a high-powered rifle with a scope. Sand gave Danny a boost so he could climb up on the motel roof. When he got to the peak of the roof, taking up a commanding and dangerous position above the police, the snipers opened fire. Danny retreated from the roof's peak to tell Sand there were six cops out front. Robert told him to stay low.

About 100 metres away, police sniper Al Lukasewich hid in hay stacks in a farmer's field. He sighted Danny through his scope. After getting clearance to fire from his commander, Lukasewich pulled the trigger. The bullet struck Danny in the head.

At the murder trial, Crown prosecutors Bob Morrison and Jim Ross portrayed Robert Sand as an evil, selfish young man who killed Strongquill simply because the police officer got in the way of the idyllic life in the Maritimes that Sand wanted to have with Bell.
Sand sees this characterization as simplistic. "I wouldn't say I was evil," he says. "Evil can't love. Evil can't care. And Laurie showed me that I can love, and I have cared about lots of things.

"I never said what I have done has been right or good," he continues. "People think, 'Oh, this guy killed a cop, he's got to be evil and twisted and whatever.' But the difference is I see someone that kills a child or a woman or someone defenceless as more evil and twisted."
In Sand's view, he was a soldier in a war.

Sand understands there are gaps in his rationalizations about the police. Even if he is enraged at certain police officers for their roughhouse tactics, why take that out on Const. Dennis Strongquill?
This last question haunts Sand. At one point in the interview, recalling the fatal gunfight, he chokes up.

"A cop got killed," he says. "You know what the worst part is? The guy has got six kids. And from what I hear he wasn't even the cop I despised, the type of cop that I've grown to hate over the years.
"From what I hear, he was a decent man."
